title: Roles, users and groups, and how they differ from the operating system’s

videos.script: Every connection to a database arrives as somebody. {{door}} The operating system has its users, and PostgreSQL keeps a list of its own, called roles. They are two lists. On your server they share a name only because lesson 3 made them match. {{two}} A role can be a person, an application, or a group of other roles. It is the same object every time, and one attribute, LOGIN, decides whether anybody can connect as it. {{groups}} In this lesson you create three: a group for reporting, an analyst called bruno, and an application. You put bruno in the group, and meet the three options PostgreSQL 16 attaches to that membership. {{options}} Then you log in as bruno for real, from your own shell, with a map that tells the server which operating-system user may be which role. And you give the application a password the way a password should be given. Never typed into a statement. Kept in a file only you can read. {{password}} By the end, you can say of any session who logged in, whose privileges it is using, and why the server let it in. {{title}}
